\# Ghost in the Pipeline — MSX 3D Maze Reborn\
\
\## Mission\
\
Build a small, visually compelling open-source application for the Hacktoberfest 2026 \*\*Ghost in the Machine\*\* challenge.\
\
Reimagine the gameplay of a classic MSX BASIC maze game as a modern Java application built with \*\*The Pipeline Framework (TPF)\*\*, then allow an AI agent to play it.\
\
The project should demonstrate that a piece of 1980s computing history can be revisited through modern application architecture, while an AI player interacts with the same deterministic game rules as a human.\
\
\*\*Working title:\*\* Ghost in the Pipeline\
\
\*\*Reference:\*\* https\://github.com/antor44/3dmaze\
\
\*\*Primary success criterion:\*\* A human and an AI can play the maze in an attractive retro-style interface, and the entire experience can be demonstrated in a short video.\
\
This is a nostalgic engineering experiment, not a production game or a generic retrocomputing platform.\
\
\## Background\
\
The project originates from my experience with 1980s home computers, particularly the Sinclair Spectrum, MSX, and Commodore 64.\
\
I want to revisit that era using the modern Java pipeline framework I've spent years developing.\
\
The result should preserve the appeal of 8-bit gaming while illustrating what modern typed pipelines, deterministic execution, and AI agents can bring to the experience.\
\
The original game should remain recognizable as the inspiration.\
\
\## Core requirements\
\
\### 1. Understand the original game\
\
Inspect the reference repository and its MSX BASIC implementation.\
\
Identify:\
\
\- Maze representation and generation\
\- Player movement\
\- Direction and first-person perspective\
\- Victory and failure conditions\
\- Level progression\
\- Limits on revisiting rooms\
\- Scoring or other relevant mechanics\
\
Identify which mechanics can reasonably be reproduced within the project's time constraints.\
\
Document any intentional simplifications.\
\
Do not build an emulator, BASIC interpreter, or general-purpose transpiler.\
\
\### 2. Intellectual property and licensing\
\
The upstream repository describes the game as free but does not establish a clear open-source redistribution license.\
\
Treat its source, graphics, packaged binaries, and any embedded system ROMs as having unresolved redistribution rights.\
\
Do not copy third-party source files, ROMs, binary artifacts, or graphical assets into the published application without appropriate permission.\
\
Implement the maze mechanics independently, using original Java code and independently created visuals.\
\
Do not assume that translating BASIC directly into Java eliminates derivative-work copyright concerns.\
\
Include a short attribution and provenance notice identifying the historical inspiration, what was independently implemented, and any unresolved rights.\
\
Flag any licensing concern before publication rather than silently asserting that the entire project is MIT- or GPL-compatible.\
\
\### 3. TPF application architecture\
\
The game rules must be deterministic.\
\
Movement validation, collision detection, level progression, and victory conditions belong to application logic, not the LLM.\
\
The same gameplay pipeline must accept actions from either a human or an AI player.\
\
Prefer pure transformations of immutable state where practical.\
\
A locally running monolithic application is preferred.\
\
\### 4. AI gameplay\
\
Introduce an AI-controlled player using TPF's existing agentic capabilities.\
\
The agent receives a structured observation of the current game state and chooses an action from a finite set.\
\
For example:\
\
\- Turn left\
\- Turn right\
\- Move forward\
\- Move backward, if supported\
\
Use a configurable inference provider.\
\
Prefer \*\*Tev1 through Ollama\*\* (0.8B) as the initial local decision model if its existing TPF integration supports the required decision shape.\
\
Other compatible models may be used if Tev1 proves unsuitable.\
\
The model must make actual gameplay decisions. Do not script a successful route and present it as autonomous AI.\
\
However, do not ask the model to interpret screenshots if structured game state is already available.\
\
The AI should not have direct write access to game state. It proposes actions; TPF validates and executes them.\
\
Bound inference calls, movement counts, and execution duration.\
\
\### 5. Make the AI experiment meaningful\
\
Measure how well the model actually plays.\
\
Capture:\
\
\- Decisions made\
\- Decision latency\
\- Invalid or rejected actions\
\- Repeated positions\
\- Rooms explored\
\- Whether the exit was found\
\- Number of moves required\
\
Compare the AI against a simple deterministic baseline, such as random legal movement or a basic exploration strategy.\
\
Do not claim that the AI is intelligent or effective merely because it can select actions.\
\
If Tev1 repeatedly gets lost, explain why and document the result.\
\
A failed escape attempt can still make an interesting demonstration.\
\
\### 6. Visual presentation\
\
This is a visually oriented Hacktoberfest submission.\
\
Create an attractive retro MSX-inspired interface with:\
\
\- A first-person maze view\
\- A recognizable 8-bit aesthetic\
\- Keyboard controls for human play\
\- AI play/pause controls\
\- Visible current level and game status\
\- A compact display of the AI's latest action and decision time\
\
The primary focus should remain the game.\
\
Avoid elaborate dashboards, generic AI chat interfaces, or large amounts of technical text during gameplay.\
\
The graphics should be independently generated rather than copied from upstream.\
\
A browser-based UI served by the Java application is acceptable.\
\
\### 7. Original and modern implementations\
\
Where practical, provide instructions for running the historical game separately in openMSX or WebMSX.\
\
The original execution is reference material, not a required component of the modern application's runtime.\
\
The new game should run independently.\
\
If the emulator can be used to validate a specific original behavior, document the comparison.\
\
Do not make emulator integration a prerequisite for completing the playable TPF application.\
\
\### 8. Open-source AI and MCP\
\
The Hacktoberfest challenge accepts open-source AI frameworks and agent harnesses, not only open-weight models.\
\
The role of TPF's open-source agentic infrastructure should therefore be clear.\
\
Use the existing TPF model connector and agentic execution capabilities for the AI player.\
\
If there is a natural, inexpensive opportunity to exercise TPF's MCP support—for example, through a narrowly scoped emulator or game-inspection tool—include it.\
\
But do not build an MCP server merely to satisfy a feature checklist.\
\
The finished application must be understandable without prior knowledge of TPF.\
\
\## Verification\
\
Implement automated tests for the deterministic game rules.\
\
Include:\
\
\- Valid and invalid movement\
\- Maze boundaries\
\- Collision behavior\
\- Level transitions\
\- Win/loss conditions\
\- Deterministic state transitions\
\- AI action validation\
\- Bounded AI execution\
\
Include at least one integration test with a real AI provider if the environment permits.\
\
Avoid asserting exact model output.\
\
Retain evidence of actual gameplay and model behavior.\
\
\## Deliverables\
\
1\. A working, locally runnable TPF application\
2\. Human-playable retro maze\
3\. AI-controlled gameplay mode\
4\. Automated tests\
5\. Reproducible AI evaluation\
6\. Concise README with screenshots and setup instructions\
7\. Attribution and licensing notice\
8\. Short architecture explanation\
9\. Draft DEV Community submission for Hacktoberfest Week 4\
10\. A reproducible demonstration suitable for a 60–90-second screen recording\
\
\## Development-session evidence\
\
Preserve meaningful development checkpoints so the Codex and TPF authoring-skill workflow can be inspected afterwards.\
\
Use commits to separate significant achievements where practical:\
\
\- Game mechanics\
\- Playable interface\
\- AI player\
\- Testing and final demonstration\
\
Review recorded development-session material for secrets and private context before publishing.\
\
\## Scope exclusions\
\
Do not build:\
\
\- A BASIC-to-Java compiler\
\- An MSX emulator\
\- A complete arcade game engine\
\- Multiplayer networking\
\- Cloud deployment infrastructure\
\- A complex AI training system\
\- A generic MCP platform\
\- A new TPF runtime\
\- A production game distribution platform\
\
Do not modify TPF merely to accommodate the demo unless a genuine framework defect blocks the application.\
\
\## Implementation instructions\
\
Inspect the current TPF capabilities, project authoring skill, relevant examples, and the historical reference before implementation.\
\
Keep the project small enough to complete within the Hacktoberfest window.\
\
Prefer a finished, playable game with an imperfect AI player over a technically elaborate architecture that cannot be demonstrated.\
\
If the original game's mechanics make the scope impractical, implement a clearly attributed, simplified first-person maze inspired by the same era.\
\
Do not conceal significant limitations.\
\
\## Definition of done\
\
A human can play a recognizable MSX-inspired first-person maze through a modern TPF application.\
\
An AI player can observe the same game state and choose legal actions using actual inference.\
\
The result is visually appealing, testable, reproducible, and suitable for a short video.\
\
The original game's historical provenance is acknowledged without claiming unverified redistribution rights.\
\
\*\*Ghost in the Pipeline: A maze from the 1980s, a Java framework from 2026, and an AI trying to find its way out.\*\*

# TPF Rapid Demo Implementation Skill

## Purpose

Implement an already-qualified TPF demo from its approved Demo Implementation Plan.

The goal is **not production software**. The goal is a small, convincing, reproducible application demonstrating the agreed business process end-to-end.

Use the canonical TPF Authoring Skill for all normal TPF implementation guidance.

## Inputs

Require:

- qualified verdict;
- Demo Implementation Plan;
- agreed demo scenario;
- supplied or synthetic test data;
- expected result;
- assumptions and exclusions;
- required customer-visible evidence.

If these are inconsistent or materially incomplete, stop.

## Rules

### Follow the approved plan

Implement the agreed demo, not the imagined full product.

Do not add speculative features, abstractions, infrastructure or production hardening.

Prefer existing TPF capabilities.

### Work autonomously

Make ordinary implementation decisions without asking questions.

Ask only when:

- business requirements are genuinely ambiguous or contradictory;
- credentials/access are required;
- proceeding would materially change the agreed demo;
- a missing TPF capability blocks the plan.

Record every human intervention.

### Handle TPF gaps explicitly

If something appears unsupported by TPF:

1. Verify that the capability really does not exist.
2. If a trivial application-level adaptation is sufficient, use it and record it.
3. If a reusable TPF enhancement appears necessary, stop and report it before modifying TPF.
4. If substantial framework work is required, stop the demo.

Do not hide framework gaps behind brittle customer-specific code.

## Declare execution topology before implementation

Before implementing a non-trivial TPF demo, declare its expected execution topology.

Identify:
- each external stimulus;
- the root execution caused by each stimulus;
- any external resume/re-entry points;
- nested pipeline composition and recursion;
- Query and Command operations;
- Await or Expansion boundaries where applicable;
- persistence and other configured aspects.

State the expected number of root executions explicitly.

Internal pipeline composition, nested pipelines, recursive iterations, Query/Command operations, persistence, projections, and ordinary processing do not create additional root executions.

Do not proceed with a design that uses repeated `PipelineExecutionService` calls to model internal stages of one logical execution. `PipelineExecutionService` belongs at external application boundaries.

## Validate the topology early

Validate execution topology on the thinnest working vertical slice before expanding the demo.

1. Implement the minimum path capable of exercising the intended topology.
2. Use GitNexus or direct structural inspection to check for unintended internal callers of `PipelineExecutionService` and similar application-level orchestration seams.
3. Run the slice using standard TPF observability.
4. Verify that root executions, resumes, nesting, and ordering match the declared topology.
5. Only then expand the scenario.

## Demo data

Use sanitized customer data or representative synthetic fixtures.

The data must be:

- safe;
- deterministic;
- reproducible;
- small enough to understand;
- sufficient to demonstrate the agreed process.

Never require live production data.

## End-to-end scenario

Create at least one named automated E2E scenario that:

1. resets demo state;
2. loads demo input;
3. executes the complete agreed workflow;
4. verifies the expected result;
5. terminates in a useful customer-visible state.

Passing compilation or unit tests is not sufficient.

## Telemetry requirement

Telemetry is mandatory for the final demo execution.

Enable Quarkus OpenTelemetry and TPF’s built-in file replay exporter during the final E2E run. Treat the resulting per-root JSON files as the authoritative TPF telemetry. Assert their number against the declared root-execution budget. If the viewer requires one dataset, merge the native replay documents without translating or replacing their topology and lifecycle events.
Do not include secrets or sensitive data.

## Customer-visible demo

The result must be understandable without reading source code.

Use whichever surface the approved plan requires:

- UI;
- generated artifact;
- API/CLI result;
- report;
- other explicit business output.

Optimize any UI for demonstrating the process, not completeness.

## Recording readiness

Provide a deterministic way to reproduce the demo.

Prefer one command or short documented sequence that:

1. resets state;
2. starts required components;
3. loads fixtures;
4. executes the E2E scenario;
5. leaves the application in a useful final state.

The demo should be easy to screen-record manually.

Do not implement video recording machinery.

## Production boundary

Do not silently productionize the demo.

Document likely follow-on work such as:

- deployment;
- production persistence;
- authentication/authorization;
- secrets;
- tenant isolation;
- backups/recovery;
- observability hardening;
- scaling/HA;
- CI/CD;
- production integrations;
- migration;
- compliance/security.

## Internal metrics

Record:

- implementation start/end;
- agent implementation time;
- total elapsed time;
- human interventions;
- clarification questions;
- build/test repair cycles;
- TPF gaps discovered;
- customer-specific adaptations;
- integrations exercised;
- E2E result.

These metrics evaluate whether Rapid Demo delivery is repeatable.

They are not customer-facing.

## Stop conditions

Stop rather than expanding scope when:

- the approved plan proves materially incorrect;
- a significant TPF gap is discovered;
- required access is unavailable;
- substantial new integration/framework work becomes necessary;
- business ambiguity prevents a defensible implementation;
- the demo requires production-grade machinery merely to function;
- there is no longer a credible bounded path to the agreed result.

Stopping early is correct behavior.

## Definition of Done

SUCCESS requires all of:

- agreed workflow works end-to-end;
- expected business result is produced;
- automated E2E scenario passes;
- demo is reproducible;
- required customer-visible surface works;
- telemetry was captured;
- Demo Execution Dataset was exported;
- demo is recording-ready;
- limitations and productionization work are documented.

## Final output

Produce:

1. working demo;
2. automated E2E scenario;
3. demo fixtures;
4. Demo Execution Dataset;
5. concise Demo README;
6. recording-ready run instructions;
7. productionization notes;
8. internal implementation metrics.

Finish with:

### Demo result
SUCCESS / STOPPED

### Demonstrated process
...

### How to run
...

### Evidence dataset
...

### Human interventions
...

### TPF gaps
...

### Limitations
...

### Productionization path
...

### Internal metrics
...

Never declare SUCCESS unless the E2E scenario actually passed.

<proposed_plan>
# Ghost in the Pipeline — bounded implementation plan

## Summary and qualification gate

Build in the existing `ghost-in-the-pipeline` repository: one locally running Java/Quarkus application, deterministic TPF gameplay, an original retro browser interface, and genuine model-driven play.

The agreed scope is a faithful three-level adaptation. The AI receives local observations and explored-room memory. Pause finishes the current bounded turn before returning control.

Before expanding implementation, satisfy the demo-implementation skill’s missing qualification prerequisite with a thin vertical slice: compile the actual pipeline, obtain one real model decision through TPF, apply it through the shared rules, display the resulting frame, and verify native replay topology. Record the verdict and approved implementation contract. Stop if substantial framework changes are required.

Use Java 21-compatible code and the current published TPF `26.10.1-SNAPSHOT` family. Freeze resolved artifact versions and checksums, and verify behavior against their matching sources; the documentation service currently stops at `26.9.2`.

## Gameplay and presentation

- Independently implement connected, seeded mazes using randomized depth-first generation. Levels contain 3×3, 4×4, and 6×6 rooms, one boundary exit, and a reproducible starting position and orientation.
- Support `FORWARD`, `TURN_LEFT`, and `TURN_RIGHT`, matching the original movement vocabulary. Turns rotate 90 degrees; walls reject forward movement.
- Use the original medium-difficulty entry allowance: each room starts with seven remaining entries; entering decrements it, and reaching zero loses the game. Spawning, turns, and collisions consume no entries.
- Crossing the designated exit advances the level; escaping level three wins. Terminal states reject further gameplay actions.
- Document the intentional changes: independent generator, seeded randomness, finite campaign, no numeric score, and omission of the original map-help allowance, directional sound hints, and extensive setup menus. Preserve the historical behavior findings with source references and BASIC line numbers. [Historical listing](https://github.com/antor44/3dmaze/blob/main/3dmaze)
- Create original SVG/canvas geometry with a dark MSX-inspired palette, bright perspective walls, pixel-style typography, a visible exit, and restrained optional scanlines. Do not reuse upstream drawing coordinates, assets, music, or screenshots.
- Keep gameplay dominant: first-person view, level/status, room-entry warning, keyboard controls, AI Play/Pause, and the latest decision and latency. Use arrows or W/A/D, plus visible buttons. Respect reduced-motion preferences.
- Show “Pausing” while an outstanding decision finishes. Disable human movement during AI ownership; restore it once paused or stopped.

## TPF architecture and application interfaces

Use immutable `GameState`, `GameAction`, `Observation`, `TransitionResult`, and bounded `RunState` values. Author canonical contracts and `pipeline.yaml` before Java services.

The same nested action pipeline validates and applies human, AI, and baseline actions. Pure transformations own movement, collisions, entry limits, progression, and terminal conditions.

The AI segment uses ordinary bounded TPF recursion:

`control/budget Query → observation → model decision Query → validation → shared action pipeline → publish Command → continue/complete`

The baseline substitutes a pure action selector for the model Query. Neither player can write authoritative state directly.

Execution topology:

- New/reset game: **one root execution**.
- Each admitted human action: **one root execution**.
- Each AI/baseline Play or resumed segment: **one root execution**, containing every internal turn.
- Pause requests, state reads, and event subscriptions: **zero additional roots**.
- No Await boundary, external resume callback, Expansion, or durable game persistence. Resume starts a new bounded segment.
- Restrict `PipelineExecutionService` to external application entrypoints; verify this structurally before expansion.

Serve static UI assets from the Java application. Provide local endpoints for new game, current view, human action, AI play, AI pause, and server-sent frame events. Clients submit actions and expected revisions, never replacement state. Keep the complete maze server-side.

Use a small application-owned connector for current control/time observations and publishing authoritative frames. Maintain one in-memory session, serialize gameplay ownership, and use session-generation/revision checks to reject duplicate or stale writes, including responses arriving after reset. Document this connector as demo-specific adaptation.

## Genuine AI and evaluation

Use TPF’s existing `decision.query.jev` connector with Ollama’s decision endpoint. Its published adapter supports `/v1/systemone`; provide the required host `ConnectionResolver`, fixed local invocation scope, and local placeholder bearer value.

- Default to `tev1:0.8b`, downloaded separately during implementation. The currently installed `tev1:latest` is 4B and must be labelled accurately.
- Make endpoint and model configurable through deployment configuration. If 0.8B cannot run, use the installed 4B variant through the same connector and record the reason; poor maze performance alone is an experimental result.
- Submit one choice question with all three action alternatives. Supply visible openings, orientation, remaining entries, prior action/result, and explored-room memory. Exclude the seed, unseen topology, exit coordinates, and solver output.
- Never insert a calculated route, override a poor decision, or substitute a baseline action after model failure.
- Limit each segment to 128 decisions, at most 128 forward attempts, and 120 seconds. Set a ten-second provider timeout, disable automatic retries, and enforce an overall segment deadline and recursion safety limit.
- Count wall collisions separately from malformed/rejected decisions. Provider or schema failure ends the segment with a visible failure reason and preserves the last committed game state.

Evaluate nine fixed cases: seeds `1983`, `1986`, and `2026` at each level size. Compare Tev1 with seeded random legal movement using identical initial states, information, rules, and action budgets.

# A small game with a framework-owned loop

The application packages one Quarkus process and serves its own static browser UI. `connectors` is a build-time dependency containing immutable game values, pure rules and the tiny local session connector; `app` owns the pipeline, authored steps and HTTP host. Two Maven modules do not mean two running services.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H[Human action] --> R[One root admission]
    P[AI or baseline Play] --> R
    R --> C[Control and time Query]
    C --> B{Typed turn branch}
    B --> M[Tev1 Decision Query]
    B --> E[Observation-only baseline]
    B --> A[Human action]
    M --> V[Validate finite choice]
    V --> G[Shared deterministic rules]
    E --> G
    A --> G
    G --> F[Publish frame Command]
    F --> T{Continue or complete}
    T -->|bounded nested recursion| C
    T -->|finish| U[Result and human control]
```

TPF's existing `decision.query.jev` provider makes one decision request to Ollama. Its canonical request contains only an explicitly constructed observation. The completion projection carries trusted run state alongside the result; the model cannot replace it. Typed unions route model, action and complete branches, and native recursive composition owns iteration.

`Rules` implements seeded generation, independent solvability admission, movement, entry exhaustion, progression and victory. Human, Tev1, Random and Explorer all reach the same reducer. The solver witness is used for level admission and human test fixtures only. It is absent from the UI/API observations, model request and baseline selectors.

Memory records visited rooms, visits, remaining entry allowance and observed edges. Front, left and right edges become known on observation; a traversed rear passage is known from the movement itself. Turning can reveal the previously unseen rear. The first-person renderer and explored map use this same projection. `#` is a wall, `.` a passage, `E` an observed exit, and `?` unknown. Room identities are row-major; unseen connectivity and exit location remain private.

The host owns one in-memory session. Admission serializes player ownership and checks expected revision. Publication is a native Command with a generation/segment/revision effect identity. Reset invalidates old segments; their late responses cannot overwrite the new game. Pause finishes at most an in-flight turn and returns through a typed base case. A separate outer watchdog invalidates ownership if a segment times out.

Each automated segment is capped at 128 decisions and 120 seconds; every translation requires a decision. Requests time out after ten seconds, retries are disabled, and TPF recursion has a separate depth bound. Rendering pace is host presentation behavior, disabled during the recorded comparison. It is excluded from decision latency.

The native model binding is deployment configuration. `scripts/run.sh` supplies a native `PIPELINE_CONFIG` file with the chosen model and endpoint. No custom agent runtime, inference proxy, model-side tools, persistence, cloud service or MCP server is involved.

See [execution-contract.md](execution-contract.md) for root/lineage expectations and the bounded compiler-shape adaptation. Native replay documents remain unchanged; the verifier checks identity, nesting lifetime and ordering rather than asserting a particular file count.

# Ghost in the Pipeline 👻

**A maze from the 1980s, a Java framework from 2026, and an AI trying to find its way out.**

An independently implemented, MSX-inspired first-person maze built with [The Pipeline Framework](https://pipelineframework.org/). Play with the keyboard, hand control to a real local Tev1 decision model, or compare it with Random and a deterministic Explorer. Seven entries per room; three growing levels; no hidden map for the AI.

![The independently drawn first-person maze](docs/screenshots/game.png)

## Run locally

Requirements: Java 21+, Maven 3.9+, Python 3 for the helper scripts, and Ollama with its decision API. The recorded run used Java 25 while compiling Java 21-compatible code. Dependencies and model weights need an initial download; gameplay then runs locally without a cloud account, CDN or hosted inference service.

```sh
ollama pull tev1:0.8b
# Start Ollama if it is not already running.
./scripts/run.sh
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:8087**. Use **↑ / W** to walk, **← / A** and **→ / D** to turn. Play/Pause hands control to the selected automated player; Pause finishes at most the current turn. Reset restarts the selected seed. An observed-only map and entry bars help you keep your bearings.

The levels are 3×3, 4×4 and 6×6. Each room starts with seven entries; entering decrements its allowance and reaching zero loses. Spawning, turning and bumping into a wall consume none. Cross the exit to advance; escape the third level to win. Every admitted level is checked for a valid escape under these same rules.

A second launch can reuse the package with `./scripts/run.sh --no-build`. Change the port with `GHOST_PORT=8089`. A compatible local model/endpoint can be selected with `GHOST_MODEL` and `GHOST_MODEL_URL`; the launcher writes a native TPF deployment binding through `PIPELINE_CONFIG`. The supplied host connection is for local Ollama, not hosted credential management.

## Test and compare

```sh
mvn -B -ntp verify
mvn -B -ntp verify -Dghost.live=true  # Includes real Tev1 inference; Ollama must be running.

# With the application running:
python3 scripts/evaluate.py
./scripts/recording-reset.sh
```

The ordinary test suite uses real TPF gameplay and observation-only baselines. The opt-in live test validates genuine model decisions without requiring an escape or an exact action. The completed delivery run passed **16 tests**, including human completion of all three levels, pause, limits, action validation and live Tev1. Core tests validate **600 seeded levels**.

Evaluation uses the same nine seed/level combinations for all players, with 128 decisions and 120 seconds per case. For timings without the visual pause, restart with `GHOST_PACE_MS=0 ./scripts/run.sh --no-build`, then run `GHOST_PACE_MS=0 python3 scripts/evaluate.py`. Do not interact with that single session during evaluation. The script leaves a fresh normal campaign ready afterwards.

| Player | Escaped | What actually happened |
|---|---:|---|
| Tev1 0.8B | 0 / 9 | Repeated forward attempts, mostly rejected by walls |
| Random legal movement | 1 / 9 | Occasionally escaped; also exhausted rooms or its action budget |
| Deterministic Explorer | 9 / 9 | Used visited-room memory and depth-first exploration |

These are small-sample observations, not a general model ranking. The maze and seeds were not adjusted to make Tev1 win. Full actions, latencies and paired starting observations are in [the evaluation dataset](evidence/evaluation.json); see [the report](docs/evaluation.md) for definitions and limits.

## How it works

One bounded TPF execution owns each automated Play segment. Typed recursive composition makes the next turn; a native Decision Query asks Tev1 for one action; the same reducer used by human play validates it. A native Command publishes the frame. The model has no state-write authority.

The model receives visited rooms, observed walls/passages/exits, entry allowances, orientation and the prior result. It does not receive unseen topology, the maze seed, the validation witness or a computed route. Explorer uses those same observations, not the solver.

See [architecture](docs/architecture.md), [execution contract](docs/execution-contract.md), and [bounded qualification](docs/qualification.md). Published TPF snapshot binaries are pinned by timestamp; [dependency identities and SHA-256 values](evidence/dependencies.json) record what was exercised. No TPF runtime changes were made. MCP was unnecessary and is omitted.

## Record and inspect

The primary deliverable is the game. Follow [the 60–90-second recording sequence](docs/recording.md); [the DEV submission](docs/dev-submission.md) is a draft, with the final video and reviewed session link still to insert. No video was recorded or uploaded automatically.

Native replay goes to `target/replay/` by default. Set `GHOST_REPLAY_PATH` to an absolute directory for a separate run. [The execution dataset](evidence/README.md) includes representative native documents and root/lineage verification:

```sh

```

## How I Built It

The Pipeline Framework, the open-source Java framework I've spent years developing, owns the execution. A typed recursive pipeline carries immutable game state through bounded turns. Its existing decision connector asks Tev1 through Ollama for one finite-choice action. Application logic validates the proposal and applies the same rules a human faces.

The model sees structured exploration memory: visited rooms, observed openings and exits, orientation, and entry allowances. It never receives a hidden map or a route from the solver. The solver only checks that a generated level has a valid escape before admitting it.

I used Codex with the TPF authoring and demo-implementation skills, preserved meaningful development commits, and checked both deterministic rules and real provider behavior. Native TPF replay records make it possible to inspect how the agent's turns stayed inside one execution. I did not add a new framework runtime or an artificial MCP layer.

And the model's performance? In nine fixed seed/level cases, Tev1 escaped **zero**. Random legal movement escaped **one**. A deterministic explorer using observed-room memory escaped **all nine**.

Tev1 repeatedly selected forward even when the observation described a wall. The rules rejected those moves. That is the observed failure mechanism; the experiment does not establish whether encoding, prompt wording, option-order bias or the model itself caused it. A valid action label is not evidence of useful navigation.

After the initial dependencies and weights are downloaded, this game and its inference run on the laptop. There is no hosted model bill or cloud account required for the default setup. I can inspect the framework, replace the model binding, read every proposed action, and rerun the comparison.

I’m retaining those runs as prior-build diagnostics and rerunning both models from the verified current package. The final report will use the corrected run.
